outlooks.summary: Severe thunderstorms with damaging winds, very large hail and a tornado or two are expected from central Montana into western North Dakota on Tuesday. A few severe storms are also possible from the Ohio Valley into parts of New England.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: An upper-level trough over the Pacific Northwest early Tuesday will evolve into an upper low as it lifts northeast across the northern Rockies and Saskatchewan Province. An associated surface low and cold front will move from central MT east into western ND Tuesday afternoon and night. An upper-level trough over eastern Canada and the northeast U.S. will sharpen somewhat as it moves east, while a surface cold front moves east/southeast from New England southwest into the Ohio Valley. Upper-level high pressure will extend across much of the remainder of the CONUS, with a couple of mid-level impulses moving west/northwest on the southern periphery of the ridge.

sections.title: Northern Rockies/adjacent high Plains
sections.text: Surface low pressure over central MT early Tuesday will move generally east in tandem with the cold front, moving into western ND/northwest SD Tuesday night. A warm front will extend east from the surface low and lift northeast during the afternoon and overnight. Intense diurnal heating of a very moist air mass and steeper mid-level lapse rates as compared to Monday will contribute to moderate/strong surface-based instability. Scattered thunderstorms should develop across western/central MT as the cold front moves east and as height falls/large-scale ascent develops. Deep-layer shear averaging 40-50 kts will favor supercells initially, and the thermodynamic/kinematic environment will support potentially very large hail along with damaging winds. The tornado risk will be maximized where the low-level flow is backed northeast of the surface low and near the warm front. This appears most likely over portions of far northeast MT north across the international border. During the evening, intensifying warm advection should lead to upscale growth into an east/northeast-moving forward-propagating MCS. sections.title: Northeast States into the Ohio Valley
sections.text: Diurnal heating of a moist air mass (surface dew points lower-mid 60s across New England to lower 70s OH Valley) will result in moderate afternoon surface-based instability. As the cold front moves southeast, height falls/mid-level cold advection should contribute to scattered afternoon/evening thunderstorm development. Moderate west/northwest mid-level flow will support deep-layer shear of 30-40 kts (strongest across central/northern New England), supporting organized storms including supercell structures with mid-level rotation capable of isolated damaging gusts. Relatively cool mid-level temperatures will also support a risk for large hail with the most intense cells. ..Bunting/Wendt.. 07/10/2018

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: The upper-air pattern over most of the CONUS should remain dominated by a persistent anticyclone initially centered over the central High Plains, with ridging west-southwestward over the Great Basin and southeastward across the Mid-South. With time, the ridging will erode from a series of perturbations -- mainly weak ones in the southern-fringe easterlies and a substantial shortwave trough now crossing the Pacific Northwest. By 00Z, that trough should be located from northern/central AB across the northern Rockies. The main associated vorticity lobe should eject northeastward across SK through tonight, but with height falls spreading across nearly all of MT and western/northern ND overnight. Height falls also are expected to spread southeastward over the northeastern U.S., from the lower Great Lakes to New England. This will occur ahead of a series of perturbations embedded in cyclonic flow, and moving southeastward from the James Bay and northeast ON regions across southern QC and the St. Lawrence Valley. sections.title: Northern High Plains
sections.text: Strong-severe thunderstorms are possible primarily in two initially separate late-afternoon regimes, each offering somewhat different severe potential in their early stages: 1. Northern area: Widely scattered to scattered rapidly developing thunderstorms in an arc located within the low-level convergence/baroclinic zone, on the cold/occluded front near the triple point, from southeastern AB across the border some short distance into MT. Risks for significant/damaging hail, severe gusts and perhaps tornadoes exists with activity on the U.S. side. Convection will shift eastward astride the international border through a very favorable environment characterized by a narrow, but eastward-shifting, corridor of rich low-level moisture and 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, amidst 45-60-kt effective-shear magnitudes. This northern convection, being embedded within stronger mid/upper flow aloft and greater magnitudes of both theta-e and shear in low levels, should contain early-stage supercells with a propensity for rightward (eastward to southeastward motion). sections.title: Northeast
sections.text: Widely scattered to scattered thunderstorms will develop along and head of the surface front through the afternoon, moving eastward to southeastward across the outlook area in a broken arc corresponding to the general shape of the front. The main concern will be sporadic damaging gusts, a few of which may reach severe limits. Isolated severe hail also is possible, especially in the middle to northeastern parts of the outlook area where cooler temperatures and somewhat greater deep shear will exist. However, overall hail size/coverage potential will be constrained by lack of greater low-level mesocyclone-supporting shear, weakness of lapse rates aloft, and decreasing inflow-layer moisture content with northward extent. Meanwhile, stronger heating/moisture will exist under somewhat weaker shear over the Ohio Valley region. Strong/isolated severe potential in this corridor will be strongly influenced by diurnal destabilization and should wane rapidly after dark. ..Edwards/Smith.. 07/10/2018

outlooks.summary: Severe thunderstorms with damaging winds and large hail are expected from central and northeastern Montana into northwestern North Dakota this afternoon through late evening. A few severe storms with damaging winds are also possible this afternoon from the Ohio Valley into parts of New England.

sections.title: MT/ND this afternoon through tonight
sections.text: A midlevel shortwave trough will move east-northeastward from the interior Pacific Northwest this morning to northern MT and southern AB/SK, around the northwestern periphery of the ridge dominating the central CONUS. An associated surface cyclone and cold front will likewise progress eastward across MT this afternoon/evening, providing a focus for severe thunderstorm development. Initial storm development is expected over the mountains of south central MT with daytime heating/mixing within the monsoonal moisture plume emanating from the Great Basin. This high-based convection will then spread east-northeastward through the afternoon/evening, likely organizing into clusters on consolidated outflow, given an environment of steep low-level lapse rates/large DCAPE and increasing midlevel flow. Other storms will also form this afternoon along the cold front in north central MT, where forcing for ascent will be stronger and deep mixing will weaken the cap. Deep-layer vertical shear will be sufficient for supercells initially, though the linear forcing for ascent and outflow interactions should lead to upscale growth into clusters/line segments. sections.title: OH Valley to New England this afternoon/evening
sections.text: A positive-tilt northern stream trough will move across New England through tonight, as an accompanying cold front moves southward into the upper OH Valley and southeastward across NY/PA and New England this afternoon through tonight. Daytime heating (afternoon temperatures in the 80s) and boundary-layer dewpoints in the low-mid 60s will drive weak-moderate buoyancy (MLCAPE of 1000-1500 J/kg). This buoyancy and straight hodographs with 35-40 kt effective bulk shear will support widely scattered storms with splitting supercells possible, and an attendant threat for damaging winds and marginally severe hail for a few hours this afternoon/evening. Despite weakening vertical shear with southwestward extent from PA into the OH Valley, downdraft potential will be strong enough to support low damaging wind probabilities with downbursts. ..Thompson/Squitieri.. 07/10/2018

sections.title: Discussion
sections.text: No appreciable changes to 1630z are warranted. Deep convection is beginning to mature off the higher terrain of south-central MT. This activity will spread northeast into a significantly more moist/buoyant air mass where intensification is expected. Supercell threat will increase across this region over the next few hours. Elsewhere, scattered thunderstorms are expected along a corridor from ME into NY and farther southwest across the OH Valley. Damaging winds are the primary threat with this convection. ..Darrow.. 07/10/2018 .PREV DISCUSSION... /ISSUED 1130 AM CDT Tue Jul 10 2018/

mesoscale_discussions.summary: An isolated, marginally severe thunderstorm is located across northwest Iowa. Hail and wind will be the near-term threat. If the thunderstorm persists into the afternoon, an uptick in wind threat will be possible. No watch is expected.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: A strong, isolated thunderstorm continues across northwest Iowa, along the southwest side of a decaying mesoscale convective system (MCS) across southern Minnesota. Although the thunderstorm has moved south/southeast of the more organized deep-layer flow, it is moving into an increasingly more favorable thermodynamic environment. Coincidentally, mesoscale flow around the periphery of the decaying MCS may locally augment the deep-layer shear in the vicinity of the ongoing convection in the short term, resulting in a small, locally favorable environment across northwest into central Iowa for organized convection to sustain itself for a few more hours. Isolated hail and wind may occur. Uncertainty increases with the thunderstorm evolution in the longer term. As the MCS continues to decay, the locally augmented deep-layer shear should diminish. However, as the deep-layer shear weakens, the thermodynamic environment should only become better with time. Given the orientation of the low-level moisture field, and the resultant instability axis, if the thunderstorm can persist into the early afternoon, the potential will exist for a small, bowing segment to evolve and push south-southeast toward the Des Moines area. In this scenario, an local enhanced wind threat would be the main severe hazard. Given the uncertainties associated with this threat, no watch is expected.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Severe potential gradually increasing over the next few hours. Convective trends are being monitored for a potential WW.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Scattered thunderstorms have developed along a cold front just north of Upstate New York and Vermont along the Canadian side of the U.S border, with new cells recently noted in Essex County, New York and Somerset County Maine. The cold front will continue to move southeast into New England, with deep-layer ascent associated with a mid-level short wave trough continuing to glance the region. As such, storms are expected to continue developing/intensifying across the area throughout the afternoon as the boundary layer continues to moisten and warm. While mid-level lapse rates are expected to remain modest (around 6.5 C/km), effective bulk shear on the order of 35-40 knots suggest that any storm that matures may become organized. The weaker lapse rates and relatively unidirectional shear suggest that damaging wind gusts will likely be the primary threat. The need for a WW remains unclear given the isolated nature of storms and convective trends will continue to be monitored.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Isolated severe is possible over the next few hours, with marginally severe hail/wind the main threats. A WW issuance is not anticipated.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Isolated storms, including a supercell with reported marginally severe hail in Piscataquis County Maine, are moving across east Maine and are expected to continue for the next few hours. Adequate deep-layer ascent and effective bulk shear suggest that the current storms will remain organized as they move across the discussion area. Marginally severe hail and gusty winds will likely be the main threats. Given the isolated and marginal nature of the storms, a WW issuance is not anticipated at this time.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Thunderstorms are developing across the higher terrain of southwest Montana. Additional thunderstorms are expected to develop farther east and north along a cold front. The environment across northeast Montana will be supportive of large hail with initial thunderstorm development with a transition to more of a damaging wind threat with time. A Severe Thunderstorm Watch is likely by 3PM MDT.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Compact shortwave trough is lifting northeast across northern Idaho and northwest Montana, with a midlevel jet nosing into central Montana. At the surface, a weak surface low located across central Montana and trailing cold front continue to move east across Montana this afternoon. The environment ahead of the surface cold front is moderately unstable, with mixed-layer CAPE increasing into the 1000-2000 J/kg range as temperatures warm into the mid-to-upper 80s F. Additionally, as the midlevel jet moves atop the region, deep-layer shear on the order of 50 knots should be maintained. Thunderstorms are now developing across the higher terrain across portions of southwest Montana with additional thunderstorms expected farther northeast this afternoon as ascent increases a during maximum heating and a frontal zone moves across the area. Given the highly sheared, moderately unstable environment in place across eastern Montana, as thunderstorms develop they will have the potential to produce large hail and damaging winds. With time, upscale growth into a mesoscale convective system (MCS) should result in an increasing damaging wind threat. A Severe Thunderstorm Watch will likely be needed by 21Z.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Isolated severe possible with scattered storms developing across the area. Marginally severe hail and wind gusts are the main threats. A WW issuance is not expected at this time.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Scattered storms continue to develop well ahead of a cold front in a broadly confluent low-level airmass across a large portion of New England this afternoon, with additional storm development possible within the next few hours. Storms will likely persist through the rest of the afternoon in association with maximum diurnal heating and associated buoyancy (MLCAPE of around 1000 J/kg). The ambient kinematic environment is characterized by deep layer unidirectional flow, with appreciable speed shear contributing to bulk effective shear values of 30-40 knots. A few of the stronger storms may become organized enough to pose a threat for isolated, marginally severe hail and wind gusts through the remainder of the diurnal heating cycle. The sparse nature of the severe threat suggests that a WW issuance is not warranted at this time.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A severe threat is likely to continue into the early to mid evening. Wind damage, large hail and a brief tornado will be possible as the storms move eastward through the central and eastern part of severe thunderstorm watch 269.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: The latest radar imagery shows a broken line of strong thunderstorms extending southward from southwestern Saskatchewan into east-central Montana. This convection is located in an area of increasing large-scale ascent ahead of a shortwave trough in the northern Rockies evident on water vapor imagery. The storms are also located along a cold front with the RAP showing a moderately unstable airmass ahead of the front across most of eastern Montana where MLCAPE values are estimated to be in the 2500 to 4000 J/kg range. In addition, the Glasgow WSR-88D VWP shows strong deep-layer shear with 0-6 km shear near 60 kt and veering winds with height in the lowest 3 KM AGL. This is a supercell wind profile and will support severe storm development this evening. Isolated large hail and wind damage will be the primary threats although a brief tornado can not be ruled out as the low-level jet intensifies early this evening.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A linear segment of severe storms has developed over the northern portions of WW 269 and currently near Glasgow, MT. These storms pose the greatest threat for severe wind gusts and isolated severe hail. A WW is probable by 02Z for areas downstream of this storm complex. Farther south/southwest, storm coverage has been minimal and little continued development is expected.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: A line of storms nearing Glasgow, MT was moving east at about 40 kts. KGGW radial velocities show 50 to near 70 kts a few hundred feet off the surface with a recent measured wind gusts of 40-45 kts in and north of Glasgow. Given a 0-6 km shear vector of around 55 kts aligned with the direction of propagation and 1500-3000 J/kg MLCAPE -- RAP analysis estimates appear to be high per 00Z GGW sounding -- ahead of the line, the expectation is for severe wind gusts to remain probable over the next few hours. Furthermore, the low-level jet is expected to increase and provide at least modest theta-E advection along the international border. Locations expected to be impacted by these storms include northeast Montana and northwest North Dakota. A downstream watch is probable in northwest North Dakota by 02Z. Farther to the south/southwest, storms have struggled to maintain organization and intensity farther away from the mid-level ascent and better deep-layer shear to the north. While some additional development may occur, the coverage of isolated severe wind gusts and hail will likely be minimal. ..Wendt.. 07/11/2018 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A wind damage threat is likely to continue for few more hours as a line of storms moves eastward across northern North Dakota. A new weather watch could be needed as the line approaches the eastern edge of the WW 270 around 0600Z although the risk should remain spatially and temporally limited.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: A well-developed linear MCS is ongoing across northwest North Dakota, which is located along a gradient of moderate instability. The RAP is estimating MLCAPE values across northern North Dakota in the 1500 to 3000 J/kg range. The line of storms is being supported by the moderate instability and by large-scale ascent associated with a shortwave trough moving eastward through the northern Plains near the top of an upper-level ridge. The WSR-88D VWP in northern North Dakota shows 0-6 km shear near 40 kt with backed east-southeasterly surface winds and strongly veering winds with height in the lowest 2 Km AGL. This wind profile will support bowing line segments within the MCS over the next few hours. A forward speed of around 50 kt will make wind damage possible along the leading edge of the linear MCS.
